questions.question: In the Monty Hall tree, the leaf (car P, pick P, host opens G) has probability 1/18 but (car P, pick G, host opens S) has probability 1/9. Why the difference?
options: The car is less likely to be behind P
In the first case the host chooses between two goat doors (1/2); in the second he is forced (1)
Leaves deeper in the tree always have smaller probability
questions.explanation: Both paths start with 1/3 · 1/3. When your pick is the car, the host splits 1/2 and 1/2 between two goat doors; otherwise only one door is allowed, so that edge has probability 1.

questions.question: A friend says: 'After the host opens a goat door, two doors are left, so each has probability 1/2.' What is the best response?
options: Correct, as long as the host chooses at random
Correct, because the tree has 6 winning and 6 losing leaves
Wrong, because the car moves after the host opens a door
Wrong: outcomes are not automatically equally likely, and adding the leaf probabilities gives 2/3 for switching
questions.explanation: Counting leaves assumes a uniform space. Here the 6 switch-wins leaves have probability 1/9 each and the 6 stay-wins leaves 1/18 each, so switching wins 2/3 of the time.

questions.question: When is it valid to compute Pr[E] as |E| / |S|?
options: When the probability space is uniform, meaning every outcome has the same probability
Always, for any finite sample space
Only when the event E contains half the outcomes
Only for events defined by dice
questions.explanation: In general Pr[E] is the sum of Pr[ω] over ω in E. If every outcome has probability 1/|S|, that sum is |E|/|S|, so probability becomes counting.

questions.question: With one roll, red beats green and green beats blue, each with probability 5/9. What can you conclude about red versus blue?
options: Red must beat blue, because 'beats' is transitive
Nothing until you compute it, and in fact blue beats red with probability 5/9
questions.explanation: 'Beats with probability above 1/2' is not a transitive relation. Counting the 9 equally likely pairs shows blue beats red in 5 of them.
